intervals__merge-intervals-insert-interv.title: Merge Intervals / Insert Interval
intervals__merge-intervals-insert-interv.pattern: Sort by start then sweep (merge); linear 3-phase scan for insert into a pre-sorted list
intervals__merge-intervals-insert-interv.statement: Two related tasks. **Merge Intervals:** given a list of `[start, end]` intervals in any order, merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping result. **Insert Interval:** given a list already sorted by start and non-overlapping, insert a `newInterval` and merge as needed.

approaches.name: Sort + sweep (merge), linear 3-phase scan (insert)
approaches.idea: For **merge**, sort by start; walk left to right keeping the last interval in the result — if the current start is beyond the last end, append it, otherwise extend the last end by `max`. For **insert**, since the list is already sorted you never sort again: copy intervals ending before the new one, absorb every interval that overlaps into `newInterval` via min/max, then copy the rest.
approaches.time: O(n log n) merge, O(n) insert

intervals__merge-intervals-insert-interv.insight: Sort by start, then a new interval only ever extends the previous one's end; for insert, the pre-sorted invariant lets you merge in one linear pass with no re-sort.

intervals__meeting-rooms-ii.title: Meeting Rooms II
intervals__meeting-rooms-ii.pattern: Min-heap of end times (or chronological start/end sweep)
intervals__meeting-rooms-ii.statement: Given meeting time intervals `[start, end]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms required so that no two overlapping meetings share a room.

examples.explanation: [0,30] overlaps both others; [5,10] and [15,20] don't overlap each other, so 2 rooms suffice.

approaches.name: Min-heap of end times
approaches.idea: Sort meetings by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of meetings currently occupying a room. For each meeting, if the earliest-ending room frees before this meeting starts (`peek <= start`), reuse it (poll); then push this meeting's end. The heap size at any point is the number of concurrent rooms, and its maximum — equivalently the final size after this greedy reuse — is the answer.

approaches.name: Chronological start/end sweep
approaches.idea: Separate and sort all start times and all end times. Sweep starts with a two-pointer over ends: each start opens a room; whenever the next-to-finish end is at or before the current start, close a room. Track the running maximum of open rooms. Avoids the heap.

intervals__meeting-rooms-ii.insight: The answer is the maximum number of intervals overlapping at any instant; a min-heap on end times reuses the earliest-freed room greedily.

intervals__non-overlapping-intervals.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
intervals__non-overlapping-intervals.pattern: Greedy: keep intervals with earliest end (activity selection)
intervals__non-overlapping-intervals.statement: Given a set of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals you must remove so that the rest are non-overlapping. Intervals sharing only an endpoint (e.g. `[1,2]` and `[2,3]`) are considered non-overlapping.

examples.explanation: Remove [1,3] and the rest are non-overlapping.
Keep one [1,2], remove the other two.

approaches.name: Greedy by earliest end
approaches.idea: This is classic activity selection: to keep the most non-overlapping intervals, always keep the one that ends earliest, since it leaves the most room for the rest. Sort by end; scan keeping `prevEnd`. If the next interval starts at or after `prevEnd` it fits (advance `prevEnd`); otherwise it overlaps and must be removed. Removals = total minus the maximum kept.

intervals__non-overlapping-intervals.insight: Maximizing kept intervals = greedily keeping the earliest finisher; removals fall out as the complement.

intervals__employee-free-time.title: Employee Free Time
intervals__employee-free-time.pattern: Flatten + sort + merge, then emit gaps
intervals__employee-free-time.statement: You are given `schedule`, a list of employees, each a list of non-overlapping busy `Interval`s sorted by start. Return the list of finite common free-time intervals for all employees, sorted, that have positive length.

examples.explanation: Merged busy time is [1,3] and [4,10], leaving the common gap [3,4].

approaches.name: Flatten, sort by start, sweep for gaps
approaches.idea: Common free time is exactly the gaps left after merging everyone's busy intervals. Pour all intervals into one list, sort by start, then sweep tracking the running maximum end: whenever the next interval starts strictly after that running end, the span between is a free interval; otherwise extend the running end. Emit each such gap.

intervals__employee-free-time.insight: Free time = the holes in the union of all busy intervals; merge everything, then whatever the sweep skips over is a free slot.

intervals__minimum-number-of-arrows-to-b.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
intervals__minimum-number-of-arrows-to-b.pattern: Greedy: shoot at the smallest current end
intervals__minimum-number-of-arrows-to-b.statement: Each balloon spans a horizontal interval `[xstart, xend]`. An arrow shot straight up at `x` bursts every balloon whose interval contains `x` (endpoints inclusive). Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons.

approaches.name: Greedy by earliest end
approaches.idea: Sort balloons by end coordinate. Fire the first arrow at the smallest end; it bursts every balloon that started at or before that point. Whenever a balloon starts strictly after the current arrow position, it needs a new arrow placed at its end. This maximizes balloons per arrow, mirroring interval-point covering. Use `long` for the arrow position to avoid 32-bit overflow.

intervals__minimum-number-of-arrows-to-b.insight: Placing each arrow at the smallest overlapping end bursts the most balloons; it's the same greedy as covering intervals by points.

intervals__data-stream-as-disjoint-inter.title: Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals
intervals__data-stream-as-disjoint-inter.pattern: TreeMap of disjoint intervals, merge neighbors on insert
intervals__data-stream-as-disjoint-inter.statement: Design `SummaryRanges`: `addNum(value)` ingests integers from a stream; `getIntervals()` returns the current numbers summarized as a sorted list of disjoint non-overlapping intervals `[a, b]`.

examples.input: addNum(1), getIntervals(), addNum(3), getIntervals(), addNum(2), getIntervals()
examples.explanation: Adding 2 bridges 1 and 3 into a single interval [1,3].

constraints: At most 3*10^4 calls to addNum and getIntervals

approaches.name: TreeMap keyed by interval start
approaches.idea: Store disjoint intervals in a `TreeMap` keyed by start with the value being `[start, end]`. On `addNum`, look at the nearest interval to the left (`lowerKey`) and right (`higherKey`): if the value bridges both adjacent intervals, merge them; if it touches or lies inside the left interval, extend it; if it is immediately left of the right interval, prepend; otherwise create a new singleton `[v, v]`. Each op is O(log n).
approaches.time: O(log n) per addNum, O(n) per getIntervals

intervals__data-stream-as-disjoint-inter.insight: Keep intervals disjoint and sorted in a TreeMap; a new value only ever touches its immediate left/right neighbor, so merging is a constant-case check around lowerKey/higherKey.

intervals__range-module.title: Range Module
intervals__range-module.pattern: TreeMap of disjoint intervals (start -> end) with floorKey merge/split
intervals__range-module.statement: Design `RangeModule` tracking half-open ranges `[left, right)`. `addRange(left, right)` adds the range (merging overlaps); `queryRange(left, right)` returns true only if every real number in `[left, right)` is currently tracked; `removeRange(left, right)` stops tracking every number in that range.

examples.explanation: [10,20) minus [14,16) leaves [10,14) and [16,20); [13,15) is only partially covered.

constraints: At most 10^4 calls total to addRange, queryRange, and removeRange

approaches.name: TreeMap of disjoint intervals with floorKey
approaches.idea: Maintain disjoint intervals as a `TreeMap` from start to end. For `addRange`, use `floorKey` on both ends to find intervals that can absorb the new one, widen `[left, right)` to swallow them, clear everything strictly inside `[left, right)`, then insert the merged interval. `queryRange` checks the floor interval covers `right`. `removeRange` re-inserts the surviving right tail and left head around the cut before clearing the interior.
approaches.time: O(log n + k) per op (k = intervals cleared)

intervals__range-module.insight: Store maximal disjoint intervals in a TreeMap; floorKey finds the interval that could contain each boundary, so add/remove reduce to widen-then-clear and split-then-clear.

intervals__maximum-profit-in-job-schedul.title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
intervals__maximum-profit-in-job-schedul.pattern: DP over jobs sorted by end + binary search for last compatible job
intervals__maximum-profit-in-job-schedul.statement: You have `n` jobs, each with `startTime[i]`, `endTime[i]`, and `profit[i]`. No two chosen jobs may overlap in time (a job ending at `t` and another starting at `t` are compatible). Return the maximum total profit obtainable.

approaches.name: Sort by end + TreeMap DP (weighted interval scheduling)
approaches.idea: This is weighted interval scheduling. Sort jobs by end time. Keep a `TreeMap` from end time to the best total profit achievable using only jobs that end by then; the map is kept monotonically increasing in value. For each job, `floorEntry(start)` gives the best profit from compatible earlier jobs; add this job's profit, and record it only if it beats the current running maximum. The last entry's value is the answer.

intervals__maximum-profit-in-job-schedul.insight: Sort by end and let a monotone TreeMap answer 'best profit among jobs finishing by my start' in O(log n) via floorEntry.

intervals__my-calendar-ii-iii.title: My Calendar II / III
intervals__my-calendar-ii-iii.pattern: Sweep with a difference map (boundary counting)
intervals__my-calendar-ii-iii.statement: Book half-open events `[start, end)`. **My Calendar II:** `book` succeeds unless it would cause a *triple* booking (three events overlapping at some point); return whether the booking was added. **My Calendar III:** every `book` always succeeds; return the current maximum *k*-booking (the largest number of events overlapping at any single point).

examples.input: MyCalendarTwo: book(10,20)=true, book(50,60)=true, book(10,40)=true, book(5,15)=false, book(5,10)=true, book(25,55)=true
examples.explanation: book(5,15) would triple-book [10,15), so it's rejected.

examples.input: MyCalendarThree: book(10,20)=1, book(50,60)=1, book(10,40)=2, book(5,15)=3, book(5,10)=3, book(25,55)=3
examples.explanation: After [5,15) the interval [10,15) is triple-booked, so the max k-booking is 3.

approaches.name: My Calendar III — difference map sweep
approaches.idea: Maintain a `TreeMap` of boundary deltas: `+1` at each start, `-1` at each end. After inserting a new event's two boundaries, sweep the map in key order accumulating the running number of active events; the maximum running value is the current max k-booking. General and returns the overlap count directly.
approaches.time: O(n) per book (n boundaries), O(n^2) overall

approaches.name: My Calendar II — track overlaps explicitly
approaches.idea: Keep two lists: all booked intervals, and the pairwise overlap intervals (double-booked regions). A new booking is rejected if it intersects any existing double-booked region (that would make a triple). Otherwise, record its intersection with each existing booking as new double-booked regions and add the booking. Intervals `[a,b)` and `[c,d)` intersect iff `a < d && c < b`.

intervals__my-calendar-ii-iii.insight: Overlap counting is boundary counting: +1 at starts, -1 at ends, sweep for the running max; for the 'no triple' variant, precompute the double-booked regions and reject anything hitting them.

intervals__the-skyline-problem.title: The Skyline Problem
intervals__the-skyline-problem.pattern: Sweep line + max-structure (TreeMap multiset), or divide & conquer
intervals__the-skyline-problem.statement: Buildings are `[left, right, height]`. Return the skyline as a list of key points `[x, height]` — the left endpoint of each horizontal segment — sorted by x. The last point has height 0, and no two consecutive segments may have equal height.

examples.explanation: Each key point marks where the tallest active building's height changes.

approaches.name: Sweep line with a TreeMap multiset of active heights
approaches.idea: Turn each building into two events: a start at its left with height `-h` and an end at its right with height `+h`. Sort by x; on ties, process starts before ends and, among starts, taller first (this is exactly what sorting by the signed height achieves). Maintain a multiset of currently-active heights (TreeMap height to count) seeded with ground level 0. After each event, the largest active height is the skyline there; emit a key point only when that maximum changes.

approaches.name: Divide & conquer
approaches.idea: Split the buildings in half, recursively compute the two sub-skylines, then merge them like merge-sort while tracking the running height contributed by each side and emitting a point whenever the combined max height changes. Also O(n log n); mirrors the segment-tree framing.

intervals__the-skyline-problem.insight: Turn buildings into start/end events, sweep left to right, and let a max-structure give the current tallest active building; emit a point only when that max changes. The tie-break encoding (negative height for starts) is the whole trick.
